subject: Biotechnology
title: Cancer Vaccines
description: A quick, practical guide to Cancer Vaccines.

hook.text: Can you vaccinate against cancer? Neoantigen vaccines teach your immune system to hunt your specific tumor.

buildup.text: Sequence the tumor's DNA, find mutations unique to it, and design an mRNA vaccine encoding those neoantigens.

discovery.text: Moderna's personalized cancer vaccine mRNA-4157 plus Keytruda cut melanoma recurrence by 44% in a Phase 2 trial.

twist.text: Every patient gets a different vaccine — manufacturing a unique drug per person upends traditional pharma economics.

climax.text: HPV vaccines prevent cervical cancer by stopping the virus — Gardasil prevents over 90% of HPV-related cancers.

punchline.text: Prevent or attack — cancer vaccines work both ways.

quiz.question: How are personalized cancer vaccines designed?
options: They use a standard protein found in all cancers
Tumor DNA is sequenced to find unique mutations, then a vaccine encoding those neoantigens is made
They are made from weakened cancer cells injected back into the patient

details.summary: Therapeutic cancer vaccines train the immune system to recognize and attack existing tumors by presenting tumor-specific antigens. Unlike preventive vaccines, they treat established cancer. mRNA technology is accelerating personalized neoantigen vaccine development for individual patients.
details.whyItMatters: Personalized cancer vaccines represent a paradigm shift from one-size-fits-all oncology. By targeting each patient's unique tumor mutations, they offer highly specific immune responses with minimal side effects and potential for long-lasting
takeaways: Therapeutic cancer vaccines train immunity against existing tumors
Neoantigen vaccines are personalized to each patient's unique tumor mutations
mRNA technology enables rapid personalized vaccine manufacturing

faq.question: How are personalized cancer vaccines made for individual patients?
faq.answer: Tumor DNA is sequenced to identify unique mutations creating neoantigens. Algorithms predict which neoantigens the patient's immune system can best recognize. A custom mRNA vaccine encoding those neoantigens is manufactured in weeks and administered to stimulate a targeted immune attack.

faq.question: Why haven't cancer vaccines been more successful historically?
faq.answer: Tumors actively suppress immune responses and create immunosuppressive microenvironments. Early vaccines targeted shared antigens with weaker immunity. Combining modern neoantigen vaccines with checkpoint inhibitors that release immune brakes is now showing much stronger clinical results.
